aion-time.line: The time the field stands in: aeons that turn at the spring-point, a moment that carries its own quality, and the law that whatever runs high turns into its opposite.

sections.title: The aeon
sections.line: Jung dates the Christian aeon to the start of Pisces and reads the coming turn as a psychological event, not merely an astronomical one.

quotes.text: the Pisces aeon is the synchronistic concomitant of two thousand years of Christian development.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: filled with intimations of a kind of enantiodromian reversal of dominants. I mean by this the dilemma of Christ and Antichrist

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: spring-point will have moved from its present position 18 degrees into Aquarius, the next aeon, that of the Water Carrier.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: We are now nearing that great change which may be expected when the spring-point enters Aquarius

sections.title: Enantiodromia
sections.line: Heraclitus' law, kept as Jung's: every development that reaches its optimum turns into its opposite — a fact of the individual as much as of an age.

quotes.text: it is used to designate the play of opposites in the course of events—the view that everything that exists turns into its opposite.
I use the term enantiodromia for the emergence of the unconscious opposite in the course of time
every psychic development, whether individual or collective, possesses an optimum which, when exceeded, produces an enantiodromia, that is, turns into its opposite
discovered the most marvellous of all psychological laws: the regulative function of opposites

What we observe here is a fundamental law of life—enantiodromia or conversion into the opposite; and it is this that makes possible the reunion of the warring halves of the personality and thereby brings the civil war to an end.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: The quality of the moment
sections.line: Time is not a neutral container: whatever is born or done at a moment carries that moment's stamp, which is what makes astrology and the mantic methods possible at all.

quotes.text: whatever is born or done at this particular moment of time has the quality of this moment of time

cite.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature

quotes.text: Fate evolves with time, and it is identical with time.

Fate and time are absolutely identical, fate being the more human aspect and time the more energic aspect. And time is another aspect of energy, for without time there is no energy, and without energy there is no time. Time is measured energy
finds itself in the psychically relative space-time continuum that is characteristic of the unconscious as such

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

sections.title: The world clock
sections.line: The most exact image Jung was given of it: a clock whose two circles have one centre, seen in a dream of 1913.

quotes.text: There is a vertical and a horizontal circle, having a common centre. This is the world clock
It is a circle, the eternal return. That is probably the historical origin of the idea of the apokatastasis, but that life is a circle is psychologically an archetypal idea

cite.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

sections.title: The turn as a system
sections.line: Read as a dynamical structure, the turn has a shape: stability that carries its own instability.

quotes.text: designates not only where a dynamic becomes unstable, but where it becomes stable as well
order is never pure. Like the yin and the yang, it carries within it the potential to turn into its opposite. The same is true for chaos

archetype-as-such.line: The keystone: an irrepresentable, purely formal model that never appears itself — only the images it pre-forms can be met, dated and compared.

sections.title: The model
sections.line: The archetype in itself is hypothetical: a formal condition of image-making, never an image.

quotes.text: The archetype as such is a hypothetical and irrepresentable model

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The archetype in itself is empty and purely formal

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: Any archetype is really perfectly indescribable, something perfectly empty, but capable of assimilating a certain kind of material of tremendous variation.

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

sections.title: The name
sections.line: The word enters Jung's vocabulary from Augustine's idea, and he never claims it as his own coinage.

quotes.text: down to Malebranche and Bacon, still stands on a Platonic footing in this respect.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The instinct's side
sections.line: The same formal pole, seen from the body's end: the archetype is what the instinct looks like from inside.

quotes.text: archetypes are simply the forms which the instincts assume

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: as the self-portrait of the instinct, in exactly the same way as consciousness is an inward perception of the objective

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: an instinct is always and inevitably coupled with something like a philosophy of life

sections.title: As many as situations
sections.line: There is no fixed catalogue: the psyche forms as many archetypes as there are recurring situations to meet.

quotes.text: as many archetypes as there are typical situations

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

collective-unconscious.line: The impersonal stratum beneath the personal one: not inherited ideas but the inherited possibility of forming them — identical in all individuals, and inferred only from what individuals live.

sections.title: The deeper layer
sections.line: The 1934 Eranos definition: a personal unconscious resting on a deeper, inborn, universal one.

quotes.text: A more or less superficial layer of the unconscious is undoubtedly personal. I call it the personal unconscious. But this personal unconscious rests upon a deeper layer, which does not derive from personal experience and is not a personal acquisition but is inborn. This deeper layer I call the collective unconscious. I have chosen the term "collective" because this part of the unconscious is not individual but universal.

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The collective unconscious is a part of the psyche which can be negatively distinguished from a personal unconscious by the fact that it does not, like the latter, owe its existence to personal experience

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: The concept's birth
sections.line: Before the name, the observation: a stratum of the unconscious that no personal history accounts for.

quotes.text: We must rather suppose that they are something like universally existent constituents of the unconscious psyche, which form, as it were, a deeper stratum of a collective nature
there are other contents which do not originate in personal acquisitions but in the inherited possibility of psychic functioning in general, i.e., in the inherited structure of the brain.

sections.title: Inherited possibilities of ideas
sections.line: The formula settles: what is inherited is not ideas but the possibility of ideas — conditions for representation, not representations.

quotes.text: There are, however, innate possibilities of ideas, a priori conditions for fantasy-production, which are somewhat similar to the Kantian categories
It is rather a question of inherited possibilities of ideas, “pathways” gradually traced out through the cumulative experience of our ancestors.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Instinct and its correlates
sections.line: The collective unconscious is not only images: it is the instincts and their correlates together.

quotes.text: there exists a second psychic system of a collective, universal, and impersonal nature which is identical in all individuals

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The collective unconscious consists of the sum of the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes. Just as everybody possesses instincts, so he also possesses a stock of archetypal images

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Inferred from phenomenology
sections.line: Its existence is never observed directly — only inferred from the forms individual experience takes.

quotes.text: This disposition I have called the collective unconscious, the existence of which can be inferred only from individual phenomenology

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: a sort of timeless and eternal world-image which counterbalances our conscious, momentary picture of the world. It means nothing less than another world, a mirrorworld if you will

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

compensation.line: The psyche's self-regulation: what consciousness leaves out returns from the unconscious, not as an enemy but as an adjustment — and the dream is where this work is done.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: Jung widens the word past Adler: compensation is not the patching of inferiority feelings but the psyche's inherent self-regulation.

quotes.text: Whereas Adler restricts his concept of compensation to the balancing of inferiority feelings, I conceive it as functional adjustment in general, an inherent self-regulation of the psychic apparatus.

sections.title: The self-regulating psyche
sections.line: The model is the body's: a system that answers imbalance with counteraction, and whose equilibrium depends on the other side being spoken.

quotes.text: Since the psyche is a self-regulating system, just as the body is, the regulating counteraction will always develop in the unconscious

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: the unconscious behaves in a compensatory or complementary manner towards the conscious

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: conscious and unconscious are not necessarily in opposition to one another, but complement one another to form a totality, which is the self

sections.title: The dream's other side
sections.line: In practice, most dreams do this work: they stress what the waking attitude left out.

quotes.text: in my experience the vast majority of dreams are compensatory. They always stress the other side in order to maintain the psychic equilibrium.
As a rule the meaning of a dream is compensatory to the conscious attitude, i.e., it adds to the latter what was lacking in it.

sections.title: Not opposition
sections.line: The word is chosen against 'contrary': the complement acts purposively, and cannot be predicted mechanically.

quotes.text: not merely mechanical or complementary, but rather compensatory
the conscious attitude of the neurotic is unnaturally onesided and must be balanced by complementary or compensatory contents deriving from the unconscious

sections.title: The ordering factor
sections.line: What arrives as compensation is often a whole figure, not a patch: the ordering symbols — mandala, quaternity — surface exactly when orientation is lost.

quotes.text: a compensatory ordering factor which is independent of the ego and whose nature transcends consciousness

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: Mandala symbols appear very frequently in moments of psychic disorientation as compensatory ordering factors

sections.title: The counteraction as a system
sections.line: Read as a dynamical system, compensation is why a stuck state cannot simply be fixed from the side that is stuck.

quotes.text: Because the shadow compensates consciousness, whenever we think we know what the shadow is, its opposite automatically begins to emerge from the unconscious

complex.line: The psyche's autonomous parts: feeling-toned knots that behave like secondary personalities — the instrument Jung found the unconscious with.

sections.title: The founding definition
sections.line: The word starts as a technical term of the association experiments: an emotionally charged group of ideas, measurable by its disturbance of reaction.

quotes.text: By "emotionally charged complex" we mean the sum of ideas referring to a particular feeling-toned event. We shall always use the term "complex" in this sense in what follows.
I found then that the experiments were almost regularly disturbed by psychic factors beyond the control of consciousness. I called them complexes

sections.title: How a complex behaves
sections.line: Not a content among contents: the complex acts as a personality, with intentions of its own, and the ego can be subjected to it.

quotes.text: The complex plays the part of a second and stronger personality, to which ego-consciousness is subjected.
This second personality devours what is left of the normal ego and forces it into the role of a secondary (oppressed) complex
because the complexes behave quite independently of the ego, and force upon it a quasi-foreign will
Complexes do indeed behave like secondary or partial personalities possessing a mental life of their own.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: What one is
sections.line: The 1934 reformulation: a complex is the image of a situation, emotionally accentuated and incompatible with the habitual attitude — which is why it has us.

quotes.text: What then, scientifically speaking, is a "feeling-toned complex"? It is the image of a certain psychic situation which is strongly accentuated emotionally and is, moreover, incompatible with the habitual attitude of consciousness.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Everyone knows nowadays that people "have complexes." What is not so well known, though far more important theoretically, is that complexes can have us.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The ground of psychic life
sections.line: Beyond pathology: the complex is the normal structure of the unconscious life, and the place where psychic energy collects.

quotes.text: The background of our consciousness (or the unconscious) consists of such complexes
directed by a psychic factor that can behave like an independent being
without complexes there can be no energy. They are the focus and very mother of energy

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

individuation.line: Becoming the whole one already is: not a title or a state but a process with two faces — an inner integration and an outward relation — and a cost the ego does not choose.

sections.title: The process
sections.line: The 1921 definition keeps it neutral: differentiation of the individual being, the opposite pole of collective psychology.

quotes.text: In general, it is the process by which individual beings are formed and differentiated; in particular, it is the development of the psychological individual (q.v.) as a being distinct from the general, collective psychology.
Individuation is practically the same as the development of consciousness out of the original state of identity

sections.title: Becoming an 'in-dividual'
sections.line: The word is made to say its own sense: an indivisible unit — one's own self — and not the ego's individuation, which is a different thing.

quotes.text: Individuation means becoming an “in-dividual,” and, in so far as “individuality” embraces our innermost, last, and incomparable uniqueness, it also implies becoming one’s own self.
In the last analysis every life is the realization of a whole, that is, of a self, for which reason this realization can also be called “individuation.”
that is, a separate, indivisible unity or "whole."

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: Two aspects
sections.line: The process is never only inner: integration and relationship are stated as equally indispensable.

quotes.text: Individuation has two principal aspects: in the first place it is an internal and subjective process of integration, and in the second it is an equally indispensable process of objective relationship
The aim of individuation is nothing less than to divest the self of the false wrappings of the persona on the one hand, and of the suggestive power of primordial images on the other

sections.title: The aim, and what it costs
sections.line: The goal is the self as an unknown centre the ego revolves around — and meeting it is a defeat for the ego, not a promotion of it.

quotes.text: Sensing the self as something irrational, as an indefinable existent, to which the ego is neither opposed nor subjected, but merely attached, and about which it revolves very much as the earth revolves round the sun—thus we come to the goal of individuation.
For this reason the experience of the self is always a defeat for the ego
but the painful experience of the union of opposites.

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: What it requires
sections.line: Nothing here can be willed into place: the dissolution of the false face is a condition, and the intention to individuate is one more face.

quotes.text: The dissolution of the persona is therefore an indispensable condition for individuation. It is, however, impossible to achieve individuation by conscious intention

libido.line: Psychic energy, de-sexualized: an energy-value that can flow into any field of activity, canalized by the archetypes as water is by river-beds — and daemonic wherever it exceeds the ego.

sections.title: The redefinition
sections.line: Jung's decisive break with Freud is stated in one sentence: libido is an energy-value, not a specific instinct.

quotes.text: We would be better advised, therefore, when speaking of libido, to understand it as an energy-value which is able to communicate itself to any field of activity whatsoever, be it power, hunger, hatred, sexuality, or religion, without ever being itself a specific instinct.

sections.title: The energic viewpoint
sections.line: The concept is deliberately modelled on physics: psychic phenomena are read as energy and its differences of potential.

quotes.text: All psychological phenomena can be considered as manifestations of energy, in the same way that all physical phenomena have been understood as energic manifestations ever since Robert Mayer discovered the law of the conservation of energy.
the concept of libido in psychology has functionally the same significance as the concept of energy in physics since the time of Robert Mayer

sections.title: Not one instinct
sections.line: The definition is one-sided precisely because the phenomena are not: no single instinct accounts for the mass of psychic life.

quotes.text: The very fact that it is impossible to derive the whole mass of psychic phenomena from a single instinct forbids a one-sided definition of “libido.”

sections.title: Canalization
sections.line: Energy is not spent but converted: symbols and archetypes are the forms along which it flows, and sacrifice is the price of a higher channel.

quotes.text: the archetypes are the forms or river-beds along which the current of psychic life has always flowed
The symbols act as transformers, their function being to convert libido from a “lower” into a “higher” form.
The sacrifice is the very reverse of regression—it is a successful canalization of libido into the symbolic equivalent of the mother, and hence a spiritualization of it

sections.title: The charge
sections.line: The concept's primitive ancestors were not theories but experiences: mana is the sensed dynamism from which the energy concept grew, and the libido itself is God and devil at once.

quotes.text: We cannot escape the impression that the primitive view of mana is a forerunner of our concept of psychic energy and, most probably, of energy in general.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: As a power which transcends consciousness the libido is by nature daemonic: it is both God and devil

The expressions, therefore, used by James show clearly that the difference between the types is the result of a different localization of the libido, this “magical power” in the depth of our being, which, depending on the individual, is directed sometimes to our inner life, sometimes to the objective world.

sections.title: The current as a system
sections.line: Read as a dynamical system, the libido is an alternating current between consciousness and the unconscious.

quotes.text: a kind of alternating current between consciousness and the unconscious

mana.line: The sensed dynamism older than any theory of it: an extraordinary effectiveness that can attach to persons and things — Jung's bridge from primitive energetics to psychic energy.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: The word arrives from ethnology with a deliberately vague sense — 'extraordinarily effective' — and Jung keeps the vagueness.

quotes.text: In his classic study of mana Lehmann defines it as something "extraordinarily effective."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: We cannot escape the impression that the primitive view of mana is a forerunner of our concept of psychic energy and, most probably, of energy in general.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: An experience, not a concept
sections.line: Mana is not a primitive theory of energy but the perception of a relation — it is present in the moment something shows itself as more than itself.

quotes.text: In the face of something extraordinary it is not he who is astonished, but rather the thing which is astonishing.
Mana is a universal medicinal or healing power which renders men, animals, and plants fruitful and endows chieftain and medicine-man with magical strength.
even at early levels of human consciousness man felt the need to represent the sensed dynamism of psychic events in a concrete way

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The reservations
sections.line: Jung keeps the term honest: it is a representation, not a concept, and nothing divine attaches to it.

quotes.text: Thus mana is not a concept but a representation based on the perception of a "phenomenal" relationship.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: nothing "divine" attaches to mana, so that one cannot see in mana the original form of an idea of God.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The mana-personality
sections.line: When the ego takes the charge for itself, the archetype is worn as a person: the magician, the great man, the woman who knows.

quotes.text: It corresponds to a dominant of the collective unconscious, to an archetype which has taken shape in the human psyche through untold ages of just that kind of experience.

sections.title: Mana now
sections.line: The word never leaves Jung's late vocabulary: conscience itself is a manifestation of it.

quotes.text: Conscience is a manifestation of mana, of the “extraordinarily powerful,” a quality which is the especial peculiarity of archetypal ideas.
The deepening and broadening of his consciousness produce the kind of effect which the primitives call “mana.”

numinosum.line: The seizing quality in religious experience: a dynamic agency that takes hold of the subject rather than being produced by will — Otto's word, kept exactly because it names the experience and not its cause.

sections.title: The term
sections.line: Jung takes the word from Otto and quotes his definition almost whole: religion is the careful observation of what seizes the subject.

quotes.text: On the contrary, it seizes and controls the human subject, who is always rather its victim than its creator.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: The numinosum is either a quality belonging to a visible object or the influence of an invisible presence that causes a peculiar alteration of consciousness.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: the attitude peculiar to a consciousness which has been changed by experience of the numinosum

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: What it does to a person
sections.line: The experience is described from inside: criticism fails, the will is paralysed, and the ego meets something greater than itself.

quotes.text: the numinosum, to use an apt expression of Rudolf Otto's

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: An integral component of any nocturnal, numinous experience is the dimming of consciousness, the feeling that one is in the grip of something greater than oneself, the impossibility of exercising criticism, and the paralysis of the will

sections.title: Never indifferent
sections.line: The presence of the numinous is always effective — healing or destroying — and it is precisely its indifference to our categories that Jung insists on.

quotes.text: the archetypes have, when they appear, a distinctly numinous character which can only be described as "spiritual," if "magical" is too strong a word

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: In a life
sections.line: In the late writings the numinous is where a life actually meets its ground: whatever comes with this intensity is experienced as such, whatever name it is given.

quotes.text: Anything that comes upon me with this intensity I experience as numinous, no matter whether I call it divine or devilish or just “fate.”
Consciousness experiences this supraordinate totality as something numinous, as a tremendum or fascinosum
I am face to face with what Rudolf Otto calls the tremendum and fascinosum. I cannot "conquer" a numinosum, I can only open myself to it, let myself be overpowered by it, trusting in its meaning

sections.title: And the doctrines
sections.line: Dogma and theology stand downstream of the experience, not the reverse.

quotes.text: As the archetypes have a “numinous” quality and underlie all religious and dogmatic ideas, depth psychology is also of importance for theology.

participation-mystique.line: Unconscious identity: the state in which subject and object are not yet distinct — the primitive stratum that never disappears from relations, and the clinical fact of the transference.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: The 1921 definition: a connection in which the subject cannot clearly distinguish itself from the object, so the relation amounts to partial identity.

quotes.text: It denotes a peculiar kind of psychological connection with objects, and consists in the fact that the subject cannot clearly distinguish himself from the object but is bound to it by a direct relationship which amounts to partial identity (q.v.).

sections.title: Identity, not sympathy
sections.line: The clearest formulations are the shortest: identity in mutual unconsciousness, and nothing mystical about it.

quotes.text: To put it briefly, it means a state of identity in mutual unconsciousness.
There is nothing “mystical” about identity, any more than there is anything mystical about the metabolism common to mother and embryo.
Lévy-Bruhl has coined the expression participation mystique for these remarkable relationships. It seems to me that the word “mystical” is not happily chosen.

sections.title: In the clinic
sections.line: In the consulting room the phenomenon is not exotic: when the dialogue touches something essential, two psychic spheres interpenetrate.

quotes.text: It is an unconscious identity in which two individual psychic spheres interpenetrate to such a degree that it is impossible to say what belongs to whom

sections.title: In art, and in matter
sections.line: The same state explains the effect of great art and the alchemists' relation to their substance.

quotes.text: This re-immersion in the state of participation mystique is the secret of artistic creation and of the effect which great art has upon us

cite.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature

quotes.text: a state of participation mystique, or unconscious identity, arose between them and the chemical substance
In this way there came into being those intimate relationships by analogy which Lévy-Bruhl fittingly describes as “participation mystique.”

persona.line: The face put on for the world: a functional compromise between individual and society — real as a function, a semblance as a self, and a disaster when worn as one.

sections.title: The mask
sections.line: The word is taken from the theatre and kept: what is worn is not who wears it.

quotes.text: This mask, i.e., the ad hoc adopted attitude, I have called the persona, which was the name for the masks worn by actors in antiquity.

a complicated system of relations between the individual consciousness and society, fittingly enough a kind of mask, designed on the one hand to make a definite impression upon others, and, on the other, to conceal the true nature of the individual
Fundamentally the persona is nothing real: it is a compromise between individual and society as to what a man should appear to be.

sections.title: Its function
sections.line: The persona is not a fault but a function: the outward attitude, concerned with objects, indispensable and never the individuality.

quotes.text: a functional complex that comes into existence for reasons of adaptation or personal convenience, but is by no means identical with the individuality. The persona is exclusively concerned with the relation to objects

sections.title: The collective's mask
sections.line: Worn long enough, the mask stops feigning and becomes a collective truth speaking through a person.

quotes.text: It is, as its name implies, only the mask worn by the collective psyche, a mask that feigns individuality
The persona is never the true character; it is a composite of the individual's behaviour and of the role attributed to him by the public

sections.title: Taking it off
sections.line: The danger is identification: whoever becomes the role is answered by the unconscious — and dissolution is a condition of individuation, not an achievement of will.

quotes.text: The dissolution of the persona is therefore an indispensable condition for individuation. It is, however, impossible to achieve individuation by conscious intention
Anyone who is himself his outward role will infallibly succumb to the inner processes

psychoid.line: Jung borrows a word he half distrusts and ends up with the hinge of the whole field: the archetype's irrepresentable side, where psyche and matter are not yet two things.

sections.title: The naming
sections.line: In the synchronicity essay Jung names the irrepresentable side of the archetype, and says the naming is a confession of not-knowing.

quotes.text: The latter represents a psyche that is identical in all individuals.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: It cannot be directly perceived or "represented," in contrast to the perceptible psychic phenomena, and on account of its "irrepresentable" nature I have called it "psychoid."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The three reservations
sections.line: The word is borrowed from Bleuler, knowingly, and Jung states at the outset exactly what it may not be taken to mean.

quotes.text: I do so with three reservations: firstly, I use it as an adjective, not as a noun; secondly, no psychic quality in the proper sense of the word is implied, but only a "quasi-psychic" one such as the reflex-processes possess; and thirdly, it is meant to distinguish a category of events from merely vitalistic phenomena on the one hand and from specifically psychic processes on the other.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: although it is always the function that creates its own organ, and maintains or modifies it.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: although my use of the term derives from a different field of perception, it nevertheless seeks to delineate roughly the same group of phenomena that Bleuler had in mind.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The form under the image
sections.line: He sets the term to work on the image: whatever the archetypal image becomes, the psychoid form beneath it stays itself.

quotes.text: The psychoid form underlying any archetypal image retains its character at all stages of development, though empirically it is capable of endless variations.

sections.title: The ultra-violet end
sections.line: The 1954 essay places the archetype as such at the far end of the psychic spectrum — a factor that cannot be made conscious and is called psychoid for that reason.

quotes.text: The archetypal representations (images and ideas) mediated to us by the unconscious should not be confused with the archetype as such. They are very varied structures which all point back to one essentially "irrepresentable" basic form.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The latter is characterized by certain formal elements and by certain fundamental meanings, although these can be grasped only approximately.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The archetype as such is a psychoid factor that belongs, as it were, to the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Since other archetypes give rise to similar doubts, it seems to me probable that the real nature of the archetype is not capable of being made conscious, that it is transcendent, on which account I call it psychoid.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The physics parallel
sections.line: Psychology and physics both work with quantities they cannot represent directly, and Jung follows the parallel to its end: psyche and matter as two aspects of one thing.

quotes.text: When the existence of two or more irrepresentables is assumed, there is always the possibility—which we tend to overlook—that it may not be a question of two or more factors but of one only.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The identity or non-identity of two irrepresentable quantities is something that cannot be proved.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Since psyche and matter are contained in one and the same world, and moreover are in continuous contact with one another and ultimately rest on irrepresentable, transcendental factors, it is not only possible but fairly probable, even, that psyche and matter are two different aspects of one and the same thing.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Just as the "psychic infra-red," the biological instinctual psyche, gradually passes over into the physiology of the organism and thus merges with its chemical and physical conditions, so the "psychic ultra-violet," the archetype, describes a field which exhibits none of the peculiarities of the physiological and yet, in the last analysis, can no longer be regarded as psychic, although it manifests itself psychically.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Although there is no form of existence that is not mediated to us psychically and only psychically, it would hardly do to say that everything is merely psychic.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: the psyche and its contents are the only reality which is given to us ioithout a medium.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The specific charge
sections.line: A page on from the naming, the archetypes are given their working definition — formal factors, patterns of behaviour, with a charge that turns up as affect.

quotes.text: The archetypes are formal factors responsible for the organization of unconscious psychic processes: they are "patterns of behaviour."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: At the same time they have a "specific charge" and develop numinous effects which express themselves as affects.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Not localized in one person
sections.line: In Flying Saucers the psychoid archetype behaves as though it were not confined to a single person.

quotes.text: The psychoid archetype has a tendency to behave as though it were not localized in one person but were active in the whole environment.

sections.title: The correspondence
sections.line: With Pauli, Jung states the double character flatly; Pauli answers, in his own voice, that the concept cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

quotes.text: it is based on the psychoid archetype, which, as experience has shown, can be express itseII both psychically and physically.

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

quotes.text: The characteristic that is peculiar to the archetype is that it manifests itself not only psychically-subjectively but also physically-objectively

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

quotes.text: but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

sections.title: The late admission
sections.line: In the 1948 footnote Jung dates his own doubt: fifty years of collecting moved him further, not closer, to certainty.

quotes.text: Not only the findings of parapsychology, but my own theoretical reflections, outlined in "On the Nature of the Psyche," have led me to certain postulates which touch on the realm of nuclear physics and the conception of the space-time continuum. This opens up the whole question of the transpsychic reality immediately underlying the psyche.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The last word
sections.line: Writing to Fordham five years before his death, the term has become shorthand: the psychoid factor is the unconscious archetype, and never its conscious representation.

quotes.text: Synchronicity tells us something about the nature of what I call the psychoid factor, i.e., the unconscious archetype (not its conscious representation!).

synchronicity.line: Meaningful coincidence: a psychic state and an outer event bound by meaning and simultaneity rather than by cause — proposed, carefully, as a factor equal in rank to causality.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: The 1952 monograph states it in one sentence, and marks it off from mere synchronism, the bare coincidence of two events.

quotes.text: Synchronicity therefore means the simultaneous occurrence of a certain psychic state with one or more external events which appear as meaningful parallels to the momentary subjective state—and, in certain cases, vice versa.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: I am therefore using the general concept of synchronicity in the special sense of a coincidence in time of two or more causally unrelated events which have the same or a similar meaning, in contrast to "synchronism," which simply means the simultaneous occurrence of two events.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: A principle, in its own right
sections.line: The term is picked deliberately for a factor equal in rank to causality, and the coincidence is given two constituents: an unconscious image, and an objective situation that matches it.

quotes.text: I have picked on the term "synchronicity" to designate a hypothetical factor equal in rank to causality as a principle of explanation.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Synchronicity therefore consists of two factors: a) An unconscious image comes into consciousness either directly (i.e., literally) or indirectly (symbolized or suggested) in the form of a dream, idea, or premonition, b) An objective situation coincides with this content

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The meaningful coincidence or equivalence of a psychic and a physical state that have no causal relationship to one another means, in general terms, that it is a modality without a cause, an "acausal orderedness."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Not a cause, an orderedness
sections.line: The concept is protected against its own enthusiasm: it is an abstract and irrepresentable quantity, and where meaning cannot be attributed, equivalence must be enough.

quotes.text: I am only too conscious that synchronicity is a highly abstract and "irrepresentable" quantity. It ascribes to the moving body a certain psychoid property which, like space, time, and causality, forms a criterion of its behaviour.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: As soon as a psychic content crosses the threshold of consciousness, the synchronistic marginal phenomena disappear, time and space resume their accustomed sway, and consciousness is once more isolated in its subjectivity

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The coinage
sections.line: The word is Jung's own, invented for what the phenomena seemed to be: occurrences stamped by the same time content.

quotes.text: things happening at the same moment as an expression of the same time content

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

quotes.text: it was he who first started me off thinking about a possible relativity of time as well as space, and their psychic conditionality

transcendent-function.line: The function that arises between the opposites: not a compromise but a living third, produced from the tension and making the transition to a new attitude organically possible.

sections.title: The name
sections.line: The word is borrowed from mathematics — a function of real and imaginary quantities — and used with the analogy held openly.

quotes.text: This function of mediation between the opposites I have termed the transcendent function, by which I mean nothing mysterious, but merely a combined function of conscious and unconscious elements, or, as in mathematics, a common function of real and imaginary quantities.

There is nothing mysterious or metaphysical about the term "transcendent function." It means a psychological function comparable in its way to a mathematical function of the same name, which is a function of real and imaginary numbers.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: “function” being here understood not as a basic function but as a complex function made up of other functions, and “transcendent” not as denoting a metaphysical quality but merely the fact that this function facilitates a transition from one attitude to another.

It has been named the “transcendent function” because it represents a function based on real and “imaginary,” or rational and irrational, data, thus bridging the yawning gulf between conscious and unconscious.

sections.title: The transition
sections.line: It is called transcendent because it carries a person from one attitude to another without discarding the unconscious — a process and a method at once.

quotes.text: It is called "transcendent" because it makes the transition from one attitude to another organically possible, without loss of the unconscious.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The whole process is called the “transcendent function.” It is a process and a method at the same time.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: The living third
sections.line: The function is what happens when the confrontation is held: the tension produces a third thing that neither side contained.

quotes.text: The confrontation of the two positions generates a tension charged with energy and creates a living, third thing

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The secret of alchemy was in fact the transcendent function, the transformation of personality through the blending and fusion of the noble with the base components, of the differentiated with the inferior functions, of the conscious with the unconscious.
The characteristics of the tortoise are the characteristics of the transcendent function, the one that unites the pairs of opposites

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

sections.title: The method
sections.line: In practice the function is a method as much as an event: the conscious realisation of what the unconscious has produced.

quotes.text: This continual process of getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious I have called the “transcendent function,” because the confrontation of conscious (rational) data with those that are unconscious (irrational) necessarily results in a modification of standpoint.
The cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious is called the “transcendent function”

sections.title: The third as a system
sections.line: Read as a dynamical system, the function describes order emerging from tension — a result no side of the opposition could have produced alone.

quotes.text: whereby chaotic dynamics actually generate a higher order result coming out than existed going in
